title: Evaluate ingredients without relying on natural claims
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Any worker in any home-service business, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish the documented requirements for ingredient evaluation from unsupported product claims.
Demonstrate correct verify–authorise–record–escalate decisions for a customer worksite.
Describe when local legislation, product labelling or specialist review governs the task.
Explain the applicable limits and safeguards for evaluate ingredients without relying on natural claims.

instruction.heading: Why natural claims are not evidence
instruction.body: Words such as natural, plant-based, eco-friendly, non-toxic and biodegradable appear on many cleaning products, and customers often assume they mean the product is safe for every surface, every person and every place. A natural origin does not decide whether a product is safe, effective or suitable for a task. Plant-derived materials, essential oils and fragrance blends can irritate skin or airways, and acids and alkalis from natural sources can still damage stone, metal or finishes. This lesson teaches you to evaluate an ingredient from its documented evidence, and to record your decision so that it can be checked.

instruction.heading: Gather the documents before you judge
instruction.body: Start from the product, not from its marketing. Obtain the product label, the current safety data sheet (SDS) and the full ingredient or composition information the supplier provides. Check that all three refer to the same product, formulation and version, and note their dates. Read the hazard statements, the signal word, the first-aid and handling sections, the PPE advice and the disposal guidance. Where the composition is not disclosed, or the SDS and label disagree, the product is not yet evaluated and is treated as unverified until the supplier supplies the missing information. Keep the documents on file with their revision dates.

instruction.heading: Separate claims from verified criteria
instruction.body: A claim is what the packaging or sales material says. A verified criterion is a result that a recognised third party has tested against a stated standard, or a fact stated in the SDS and composition. When a product says it is certified or eco-friendly, ask what the claim refers to, which standard or test it rests on, who verified it, and whether that verification covers this formulation and this version. A manufacturer's self-declaration is useful information but is not the same as independent verification. A claim with no stated basis does not count as evidence and should not be repeated to a client.

instruction.heading: Judge exposure, surfaces and the people present
instruction.body: Judge the product by the way it will be used. Look at the concentration and dilution the approved method calls for, the route of exposure (skin, eyes, inhalation or ingestion), how long people and surfaces will be in contact with it, and the ventilation of the space. Check whether any occupant is vulnerable, such as a child, an older person or a person with asthma, and whether the client has reported a fragrance or other sensitivity. Check the surface as well: a product suited to sealed tiles may etch natural stone or damage a timber finish. Use the surface compatibility information from the manufacturer or the approved method. Where any of these points cannot be confirmed, the product is not used on that task.

instruction.heading: Decide and record
instruction.body: With the documents and the exposure picture in hand, choose one of four decisions: use the product as the approved method states, use it only with named controls such as dilution, ventilation or a test patch, refer it to a supervisor or specialist, or do not use it. Record the product, the documents checked, the reason for the decision, the controls and the person who approved it. Do not mix products to improve performance, do not raise the concentration to get a stronger result, and do not make a disinfectant claim the product does not support. A product that cannot be evaluated is recorded as not evaluated.

instruction.heading: Worked check on a fragrance-sensitive client
instruction.body: A scented botanical product is proposed for a poorly ventilated childcare area after a customer reports fragrance sensitivity. The botanical name and the natural claim do not answer the question. The evidence needed is the composition, the SDS hazard statements for the fragrance and any carrier, the ventilation and occupancy of the space, and a comparison with unscented authorised options. The right action is to pause the product, compare the unscented authorised options against the site's risk controls, and record why the chosen option was selected. The customer hears what was checked and what was not, without any claim that the product is safe for the room.

instruction.heading: Legal limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not authorise the use of any product for a regulated task. Check the label, the SDS and the employer's approved products list before any use.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop, leave the area safe and tell your supervisor before using a product if its label, SDS or composition is missing, if the documents do not match the product in hand, if a client or occupant reports a reaction or sensitivity, if the surface may be damaged, if the product would be mixed with another or used stronger than the approved method, or if a supervisor asks you to skip a verification step to meet a deadline. Do not proceed on an unverified product, claim or exposure-control method.

procedure: Identify the exact product, its formulation and its version, and note the supplier.
Obtain the label, the current SDS and the full composition, and check that all three match the product in hand.
Read the hazard statements, the signal word, the first-aid and PPE sections, and the disposal guidance.
Separate each marketing claim from verified criteria, and record what each claim is based on.
Check the intended dilution, the exposure route, the ventilation, the occupants and any reported sensitivity.
Check surface compatibility against the approved method or the manufacturer's guidance.
Choose one decision (use, use with named controls, refer or do not use) and record the reason and the approver.
If any document or check is missing, record the product as not evaluated and do not use it.

workedExamples.situation: A scented botanical product is proposed for a poorly ventilated childcare area after a customer reports fragrance sensitivity.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first safe action is to hold the product rather than use it in the room. Ask for the composition, the SDS and the label, and check the fragrance and carrier hazards against the room's ventilation and occupants. Tell the supervisor and the site contact that the product is on hold. Compare the unscented authorised options against the site's controls, and use one only once it has been checked. Record the sensitivity report, the decision and the approver, and explain to the customer what was checked.

workedExamples.situation: A product is marketed as 'plant-based and non-toxic', and the customer asks you to confirm that it is safe to use around pets and children.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you confirm the product is safe for that use?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The marketing words do not give a basis for a safety confirmation. Check the SDS and the composition for the hazard statements, the dilution and surface guidance, and any independent verification the supplier can name. If the evidence does not cover use around pets and children, tell the customer the product has not been confirmed for that use, and offer an authorised option supported by evidence. Record what was checked and what the customer was told.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence notice: completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated or restricted work. Check the licence or authorisation rules for your state or territory, and obtain your employer or site written authorisation before starting any work that is outside your training.

Stop-work rule: stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before continuing if the task is outside your training or authorisation, the hazard or the required permission is unclear, or the client asks for work that the work order does not cover.

qualityStandard: A natural or eco claim is not accepted as evidence, and each product is judged from its label, SDS and composition.
The label, SDS and composition are checked to describe the same product, formulation and version, and marketing claims are separated from verified criteria.
Dilution, exposure route, ventilation, occupants, sensitivities and surface compatibility are checked before use.
A product with missing documents is recorded as not evaluated and is not used, and products are not mixed or over-concentrated.
summary: A natural or eco claim is a claim, not evidence of safety or suitability.
Evaluate each product from the label, the SDS and the full composition, and confirm that all three match.
Separate marketing claims from verified criteria, and record what each claim is based on.
Judge the product by its dilution, exposure route, ventilation, occupants, sensitivities and surfaces.
Do not mix products or raise concentration to improve results.
Record the decision and the approver, and mark a product as not evaluated when evidence is missing.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must you verify before proceeding with ingredient evaluation?
options: The natural or eco claim on the packaging, since the brand is well known to most customers
A colleague's recommendation based on past use with a similar product on other sites nearby
The documented requirements and the current product label, not the natural or eco claim on the packaging
The product's fragrance, since natural scents are usually safe and it smells pleasant to staff

knowledgeChecks.question: What must the label, the safety data sheet and the composition information refer to?
options: The same product, formulation and version
